title: Lawmakers target Flock cameras with a threat to highway funding
gist: A bipartisan No FLOCK Act from Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Michael Cloud would make the Transportation secretary withhold 10 percent of a state's annual highway funding unless the state restricts automated license plate readers to five enumerated uses, with penalties starting October 2028. The bill stops short of a ban and does not block data sharing with immigration authorities, while Flock has quietly added a fifth DC lobbying firm and President Trump has publicly backed the cameras.

insights.claim: The No FLOCK Act would direct the US secretary of transportation to withhold 10 percent of a state's annual federal highway, road, and bridge funding if the state fails to restrict automated license plate readers, reviving the same fiscal-leverage tactic that established the national minimum drinking age and DUI standards.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Conditioning surface transportation funds is a proven, hard-to-litigate federal lever — if it advances, state ALPR restrictions arrive fast and uniformly rather than piecemeal.
insights.quote: directs the US secretary of transportation to withhold 10 percent of annual financial support due to states for highways, roads, and bridges
insights.locator: The No FLOCK Act—for Federal License-Plate Observation

insights.claim: Noncompliant states would begin losing tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual transportation funding only from October 2028, giving camera vendors and states a multi-year adjustment runway even if the bill passes this year.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Near-term revenue for license-plate-reader vendors is insulated; the cliff is a 2028 event, so contracts written now still amortize.
insights.quote: states that fail to comply with it would begin losing out on tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual transportation funding starting in October 2028
insights.locator: If the legislation is passes this year

insights.claim: The bill would confine license plate readers to five permitted uses — toll enforcement, stolen vehicles, missing or endangered persons, vehicles registered to felony warrant subjects, and felony investigations — explicitly excluding traffic studies, minor drug crimes, and parking and speeding enforcement.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The excluded categories (parking, speeding, traffic studies) are high-volume recurring revenue for camera vendors and municipalities; that is where the real dollar exposure sits.
insights.quote: enforcing toll systems, identifying stolen vehicles, missing or endangered persons, vehicles registered to persons with a warrant for a felony offense, or investigating a vehicle involved in a felony offense
insights.locator: The legislation says that Flock cameras could be used only for

insights.claim: The proposed legislation does not ban Flock systems outright and does not stop Flock users from broadly sharing license plate tracking data with other government agencies including immigration authorities, leaving the protest movement's top demand unmet.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Even a passed bill preserves the core product and its interagency data flows, so the existential-risk case against camera vendors is weaker than the headline suggests.
insights.quote: But the bill stops short of banning Flock systems altogether, which has been the number one demand from supporters of a global protest movement
insights.locator: But the bill stops short of banning

insights.claim: About 25 states and US territories already have automated license plate reader laws — mostly transparency mandates and prompt deletion of unnecessary data — but few limit permitted use types, according to NYU School of Law's Policing Project.
insights.speaker: WIRED
entities: New York University School of Law
insights.so_what: Existing state law barely constrains use cases, so federal use-case limits would be a genuine step change in vendor deployment economics rather than a codification of the status quo.
insights.locator: About 25 states and US territories have laws

insights.claim: Flock's Washington lobbying spending has been steady over the past 18 months and the company recently retained a fifth outside firm according to federal records, signaling it expects a sustained legislative fight rather than a one-off scare.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Escalating lobbying headcount is a leading indicator that management sees policy risk as durable and material to the business model.
insights.quote: Flock’s lobbying spending in Washington, DC, has been steady over the past 18 months, and it recently hired a fifth firm to help with the efforts
insights.locator: Another bipartisan bill introduced in Congress recently

insights.claim: President Donald Trump publicly told reporters he supports Flock cameras because they help law enforcement, making presidential signature the binding constraint on any restrictive ALPR legislation reaching law.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Veto risk means bipartisan sponsorship is not a passage signal; price the bill as low-probability near term despite the co-sponsor optics.
insights.quote: The president expressed support for Flock cameras on Sunday, telling reporters that they help law enforcement authorities.
insights.locator: The president expressed support for Flock cameras

insights.claim: Rogue AI systems, data center construction, and police abuse of Flock cameras have all become major topics in US midterm elections now less than two months away, putting three distinct technology sectors into direct electoral crosshairs simultaneously.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Watch data center siting and AI oversight bills as a correlated post-midterm policy basket, not as unrelated one-offs.
insights.quote: A number of issues related to emerging technologies, including rogue AI systems, data center construction, and law enforcement abuse of Flock cameras, have become major topics in the upcoming US midterm elections

insights.claim: One report found at least 100 instances of alleged police abuse of Flock footage over the past eight years, including officers using it to stalk former romantic partners — the specific evidence base driving otherwise pro-law-enforcement lawmakers to legislate.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Documented abuse counts are what convert bipartisan discomfort into bill text; expect the number cited to grow and drive further state action.
insights.quote: One report found at least 100 instances of alleged abuse over the past eight years.
insights.locator: Lawmakers largely agree, but they are frustrated
